title: Your teachers
hookLine: the people who taught you anything true

cards: A note in red pen in the margin of an old school essay: good, now say what you mean. A coach's voice from the sideline, repeating the same two words all season.
An aunt in a kitchen, measuring salt by the look of it, not the spoon. Some teachers have titles.

Some have none: a coworker, a kid down the street, a stranger on a long bus ride who told the truth when a polite lie would have been easier. Today turns the lamp toward the teachers in a life like yours.

teach.b: Today's text is the Buddha's advice to a young householder named Sigala.

As the story goes, Sigala's dying father told him to honor the directions, so each morning Sigala bows to the east, south, west, north, the sky and the earth. The Buddha gives the old custom a new meaning.
The directions, he says, are the people in your life: parents, teachers, a spouse and children, friends, workers, and religious teachers. Honor them by how you treat them. The teachers are the south.

teach.h: STUDENT AND TEACHER LOOK AFTER EACH OTHER.
teach.b: A student looks after a teacher by rising to greet them, attending on them, wanting to learn, listening closely.

Then the text turns around: a teacher owes the student good training, makes sure they've really grasped what was taught, and speaks well of them to friends. So a teacher isn't a vending machine for facts.
A teacher keeps an eye on you, checks you understood, and is proud of you in public.

teach.h: THE FRIEND WHO GIVES GOOD COUNSEL.
teach.b: The same discourse describes a true friend who sounds a lot like a teacher: the friend who gives good counsel.
That friend keeps you from wrong, encourages you in what is good, tells you what you hadn't heard before, and shows you the way to heaven. No robe is mentioned.
Learning here happens in households and friendships, not only temples. A teacher might be the monk at the local vihara.
It might be the friend who drove you to the hospital, or the boss who corrected you without shaming you. The text doesn't call every friend a teacher. It describes what the good ones do.

how: Buddhists in many places honor teachers with bows, offerings and gratitude ceremonies, and the advice to Sigala is taught in some communities as a guide to everyday relationships, teachers among them.

the monks who lead your local temple

he kept the custom and gave it a new meaning: the directions are the people in his life.
in the advice to Sigala, the teacher has duties to the student too
train them well, make sure they've grasped it, speak well of them to friends.

it describes a friend who keeps you from wrong and tells you what you hadn't heard.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a young man is bowing to the directions each morning because his dying father told him to. what do you do?
o: tell him the custom is useless.
show him the directions stand for the people in his life.
walk past; it's his family's business.
games.why: the Buddha keeps the bow and gives it meaning: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers and religious teachers, each honored by how he treats them.

practice: Let three people come to mind who taught you something true; not the most important three, just three.
For each, find the single thing they taught you in a few plain words, like she taught me to finish what I start, and hold it for a few breaths before moving on.
If someone difficult shows up on the list, that's allowed; hard teachers count too.

wordCard.voice: Your teachers. The people who taught you anything true, with or without a title. In the advice to Sigala, they're a direction worth bowing to.

orig.note: Pali disa: a direction; in the advice to Sigala, the people a person honors.

carryVoice: Your line: proud of you in public. That's what the good ones do. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the directions, pupil and teacher, the good friend
